questions.question: A 70-year-old male comes with complaints of hip pain. An X-ray of the hip shows lytic lesions and elevated serum calcium levels. Bone marrow plasma cells are 42%, and the cells seen are given in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Multiple myeloma is characterised by malignant plasma cell proliferation in the bone marrow, leading to lytic bone lesions and elevated serum calcium levels (due to bone resorption). The presence of plasma cells further supports the diagnosis. Bone Marrow Biopsy Findings of Multiple Myeloma: Increased number of plasma cells in the marrow, often >30% of cellularity.

Plasma cells may infiltrate the interstitium subtly or completely replace normal elements. HPE: Eccentric nucleus with perinuclear clearing (prominent Golgi) and abundant basophilic cytoplasm. Normal-appearing plasma cells, plasmablasts with vesicular nuclear chromatin and prominent single nucleolus, or bizarre, multinucleated cells may predominate.

Other Cytologic Variants (due to dysregulated Ig synthesis and secretion): Flame cells: Fiery red cytoplasm. Mott cells: Contain multiple grapelike cytoplasmic droplets. Inclusions: Russell bodies: Globular cytoplasmic inclusions. Dutcher bodies: Globular nuclear inclusions.

Incorrect Options: CLL (Option B) is a malignancy of mature B-cells, not associated with lytic bone lesions or elevated calcium. It shows Smudge cells (or parachute/basket cells) due to the fragility of lymphocytes during slide preparation and convent girl appearance (a lot of homogenous, small, mature-like, round lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm). ALL (Option C) affects immature lymphocytes and typically presents with other hematologic symptoms, not lytic bone lesions and elevated calcium. It shows Lymphoblasts in bone marrow >=20%, Cytoplasmic vacuolations, fat (Oil Red O Positive) and hand mirror-shaped cells. CML (Option D) is a myeloproliferative disorder that primarily affects granulocytes and is not associated with plasma cells or lytic bone lesions. It presents with Leukocytosis with cell types including Neutrophils (multilobed nucleus), metamyelocytes (indented nucleus), myelocytes (D-shaped nucleus), and eosinophils (orange cells) College girl/garden party appearance: Due to the variety of cell appearances Shift to the Left: Presence of immature cell types, mainly immature neutrophils, in the blood.

questions.question: Anaplasia refers to:

options.B: Variation in cell size and shape
options.C: Replacement of one type of cell by other

explanation.text: Anaplasia is characterized by the loss of normal cellular differentiation, i.e., the tumor cells do not resemble the parent tissue cells they originated from.
Incorrect Options: Option B - Variation in cell size and shape: Pleomorphism refers to the presence of cells with different sizes and shapes within a tumor.

Option C - Replacement of one type of cell by another: Metaplasia refers to the reversible change of one mature cell type to another mature cell type in response to certain stimuli or chronic irritation.

Option D - Disordered arrangement of tumor cells: The disordered arrangement of tumor cells is known as architectural disorder or loss of normal tissue architecture, which is often observed in malignant tumors.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about anaplasia?

explanation.text: Anaplasia refers to the loss of differentiation of cells. It is a characteristic feature of malignant tumors and is associated with the loss of normal tissue organization and cellular features. Anaplastic cells often exhibit pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, an increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and increased mitotic activity.
Incorrect Options: Option A - Loss of cohesion between cells: Loss of cohesion between cells is a characteristic feature of malignancy.
Option C - Change of epithelium type: Metaplasia refers to the reversible change of one mature cell type to another mature cell type in response to certain stimuli or chronic irritation.
Option D - Benign and fully reversible: Anaplasia is typically seen in malignant tumors and is not fully reversible.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a small round blue cell tumor?

explanation.text: Hemangioblastoma is not a small round blue cell tumor. It is a rare, benign tumor that arises from the blood vessels in the central nervous system. Histologically, it is characterized by abundant blood vessels and stromal cells. It is commonly associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease, an inherited condition that predisposes individuals to the development of various tumors.

Incorrect Options: Option B - Ewing's sarcoma: Ewing's sarcoma is a malignant tumor that predominantly affects children and young adults. It is characterized by small round blue cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. It commonly arises in the bones, but it can also occur in soft tissues. Ewing's sarcoma often presents with localized pain and swelling and can metastasize to other sites.

Option C - Retinoblastoma: Retinoblastoma is a malignant tumor that develops in the retina of the eye. It primarily affects children and can occur unilaterally or bilaterally. Retinoblastoma is characterized by small round blue cells and can cause leukocoria and visual disturbances. It is associated with mutations in the RB1 gene.

Option D - Neuroblastoma: Neuroblastoma is a malignant tumor that arises from primitive nerve cells, typically in the adrenal glands or along the sympathetic nervous system. It is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children. Neuroblastoma is composed of small round blue cells and can present with various signs and symptoms, including abdominal mass, bone pain, and neurologic changes.

questions.question: Which of the following does not fall under the provisional entity in the WHO 2016 classification of hematolymphoid tumours?

options.A: Natural Killer cell lymphoblastic leukemia / lymphoma
options.C: Acute myeloid leukemia with RUNX1 mutation

explanation.text: In the WHO 2016 classification of hematolymphoid tumors, provisional entity refers to a category that includes certain rare or less well-characterized entities where further research and clinical experience are needed to determine their precise classification and clinical significance. This is not included as a provisional entity. It has its own classification within the WHO classification of lymphoid neoplasms.
Incorrect Options: Option A, B, and C are included as a provisional entity in the WHO 2016 classification of hematolymphoid tumors.

questions.question: Which of the following proto-oncogenes is not implicated in carcinoma of the thyroid??

explanation.text: P53 is not implicated in carcinoma of the thyroid.
Incorrect Options: Option A - RAS: Mutations in the RAS proto-oncogene, particularly the HRAS and KRAS isoforms, are found in thyroid cancer.
Option B - RET: Mutations in RET are associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) syndromes, which include medullary thyroid carcinoma.
Option C - BRAF: Mutations in the BRAF proto-oncogene, particularly the V600E mutation, are found in papillary thyroid carcinoma.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common brain tumor seen in children?

explanation.text: Medulloblastoma is the most common brain tumors seen in children. It typically occurs in the cerebellum, which is the part of the brain responsible for coordination and balance. Medulloblastomas are fast-growing tumors that often present with symptoms such as headaches, vomiting, unsteadiness, and problems with motor coordination. Treatment typically involves a combination of surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy.
Incorrect options: Options B, C, and D are incorrect.

questions.question: Which of the following components is typically not included in immunohistochemistry for acute lymphoblastic leukemia?

explanation.text: Cytokeratins are a group of proteins that are primarily found in epithelial cells, which line the surfaces and cavities of the body. They are not specific markers for lymphoid cells and are not typically used in the diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

Incorrect Options: Option A - TdT: Tdt is an enzyme that is typically present in the early stages of lymphoid cell development. It is not found in mature lymphocytes but is expressed in lymphoblasts, which are the immature precursor cells in ALL. Tdt is commonly used as a marker to identify and confirm the presence of lymphoblasts in ALL. Tdt-positive staining indicates the presence of immature lymphoid cells, which is a characteristic feature of ALL.

Option B - CD1a: CD1a is a cell surface marker that is predominantly expressed on Langerhans cells, which are specialized immune cells found in the skin and mucosal tissues. In the context of immunohistochemistry for ALL, CD1a is used to differentiate T-cell ALL (which is CD1a-positive) from B-cell ALL (which is CD1a-negative).

Option C - CD3: CD3 is a complex of proteins that is present on the surface of mature T lymphocytes. In the context of immunohistochemistry for ALL, CD3 is used to detect T-cell ALL, as the malignant cells in this subtype express CD3 on their surface. CD3-positive staining helps confirm the T-cell lineage of the leukemia cells.

questions.question: NARP syndrome belongs to:

explanation.text: NARP syndrome is caused by mutations in the mitochondrial DNA, specifically in the ATPase 6 gene. Mitochondrial function disorders involve defects in the mitochondria, which are responsible for producing energy in the form of ATP through oxidative phosphorylation.
Incorrect Options: Options A, C, and D are incorrect.

questions.question: How would you distinguish between a thymoma and ALL when presented with a mediastinal mass?

explanation.text: Cytokeratins are intermediate filaments found in epithelial cells. Thymomas are tumors of thymic epithelial cells and express cytokeratin markers. ALL is a lymphoid malignancy and does not express cytokeratins.
Incorrect Options: Options A, B, and C are incorrect.

questions.question: The mutations / changes that convert proto-oncogene to oncogene include all except:

explanation.text: Enhancer deletion is not a mechanism that directly converts a proto-oncogene to an oncogene. Enhancers are regulatory DNA sequences that enhance the transcription of genes. While enhancer mutations can contribute to gene dysregulation, they do not directly convert a proto-oncogene to an oncogene.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Promoter insertion: Promoter insertion is a genetic alteration that can convert a proto-oncogene to an oncogene. When a promoter sequence is inserted near a proto-oncogene, it can lead to increased and unregulated expression of the gene, promoting cell growth and division.

Option C - Gene amplification: Gene amplification refers to an increase in the number of copies of a specific gene. If a proto-oncogene undergoes amplification, it results in an increased dosage of the gene product, leading to abnormal cell proliferation and potentially converting it to an oncogene.

Option D - Point mutation: Point mutations, which are single nucleotide changes in the DNA sequence, can convert a proto-oncogene to an oncogene. Point mutations can result in altered protein function, increased protein stability, or constitutive activation of signalling pathways, promoting uncontrolled cell growth and division.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of innate immunity?

options.B: Made of epithelial barriers, phagocytes, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) and NK cells
options.D: Has a lag phase between exposure and response

explanation.text: The lag phase between exposure and response is not a feature of innate immunity as it acts rapidly against pathogens. The lag phase is a feature of adaptive immunity. It specifically targets the pathogen causing infection, so it first needs to recognize the pathogen. This means that it’s slower to respond than the innate immune system, but it’s more accurate when it does respond.

Because of immunological memory, the next time it faces the same pathogen, there is a quick and robust response. Innate immunity is the body's first line of defense against pathogens, present since birth. It responds similarly to all germs and foreign substances, hence the term non-specific immune system.

Difference between innate and acquired immunity Innate/native immunity Acquired/adaptive immunity Present since birth (Option A) Occurs after exposure to the pathogen Quick, non-specific response (Option C) Slower, specific response to a pathogen No immunological memory Has immunological memory Examples include: Epithelial barriers like skin, GIT. (Option B) Plasma proteins like C-reactive protein.

Neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells, complement. Cells are of 2 types: B lymphocytes: Provides humoral immunity and produces antibodies 2. T lymphocytes: Involved in cell-mediated immunity and help with immunity against intracellular microbes

questions.question: A 45-year-old male presents with a fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes. He is diagnosed with a viral infection. Which of the following cells is most likely involved in the early defense against the offending agent in this patient?

explanation.text: In this scenario, the patient has a viral infection, and the body's initial defense mechanism against the virus is Natural Killer (NK) cells. Natural Killer cell (NK): Produced by a large granular lymphocyte. Constitutes 5 to 10% of circulating blood lymphocytes. Function: It can be part of both innate and adaptive immunity. Innate immunity: Directly kill the virus-infected cells or tumour cells.

Adaptive immunity: Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity. T cells ( Option B) are important in the adaptive immune response against viruses, they are not typically involved in the body's immediate defense mechanism during the early stages of infection. Macrophages and Histiocytes (Option C & D) are part of the innate immune system and play a role in the immune response to viral infections.
However, NK cells are more directly involved in the early defence against viruses due to their ability to recognize and kill virus-infected cells without prior sensitization.

questions.question: A 20-year-old medical student went for a screening health test and was injected with PPD intradermally. Identify the immune cell in the skin that picks up the PPD to present it to T cells.

explanation.text: The given clinical scenario describes the Mantoux test. Langerhans cells are specialized dendritic cells found in the skin and mucosa. They are responsible for antigen presentation in the immune system. They are part of the body's first line of defense and belong to the innate immune system. Dendritic cells(DC) are the most potent antigen-presenting cells(APC) for initiating T-cell responses against protein antigens.

Dendritic cell properties: They have many cytoplasmic processes resembling dendrites and receptors that sense microbes and cell damage that stimulate the secretion of cytokines. This has a critical role in inflammation and antiviral defense. They express receptors for capturing antigens, including TLRs and lectins. They are located under the epithelia and interstitia of all tissues, which are common sites for capturing antigens.
They have a higher concentration of MHCs and are present in greater numbers in the epidermis than other APCs. Immature DCs within the epidermis are called Langerhans cells.

**Langhans cells/Langhans giant cells (Option A):** are multinucleated giant cells found in granulomas. They consist of huge cytoplasm and multiple nuclei that are derived from the fusion of multiple activated macrophages.

**Follicular dendritic cells (Option B):** are specialized cells found in lymphoid follicles within lymph nodes and the spleen. They play a crucial role in presenting antigens to B cells and are involved in the formation and maintenance of the germinal center reaction.
**NK cells (Option D):** are not APCs. They destroy abnormal cells, such as virus-infected or malignant cells.

questions.question: Toll-like receptors are seen in which of the following cells?

explanation.text: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are a family of pattern-recognition receptors expressed on immune cells like macrophages, dendritic cells, and natural killer cells, as well as on non-immune cells like endothelial cells.

Pattern recognition receptors Receptor Type Cellular Compartment Function Toll-like Receptors (TLRs) Plasma membrane, endosomal vesicles Detect microbial components (e.g., bacterial lipopolysaccharides, viral RNA) The final effect of antigen binding to TLR is the activation of transcription factors: 1. NF-κB: Stimulates the synthesis and secretion of cytokines and expression of adhesion molecules. 2.
Interferon regulatory factors (IRFs): stimulate the production of antiviral cytokines and interferons.

questions.question: An 8-year-old child is brought with complaints of fever and burning micturition. She was diagnosed to have UTI with toxin-producing strains of E.coli. Where are blood-borne antigens trapped in the immune response to these toxins?

explanation.text: In the immune response to toxin-producing strains of E. coli causing UTI, blood-borne antigens are primarily trapped and processed in the spleen. The spleen is an important secondary lymphoid organ where circulating antigens, including those derived from bacteria and their toxins, are captured by specialized cells such as macrophages.

These antigens are then presented to immune cells, initiating an immune response to neutralize the toxins and clear the infection. The spleen is part of the secondary lymphoid organs, including lymph nodes and mucosal/cutaneous lymphoid tissues. They are a part of adaptive immunity. In contrast, primary lymphoid organs like the thymus and bone marrow are involved in the development and maturation of immune cells (T and B lymphocytes).

questions.question: Which of the following HLA gene regions encodes Class II MHC molecules?

explanation.text: Class II MHC molecules are encoded in a region called HLA-D. Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) is derived from the HLA gene that is presented on chromosome 6p. HLA consists of three regions, which have been designated as class I, class II, and class III based on the structure and function of gene products.
Gene region Encoded products Class I HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C Class II HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR. Class III Tumor necrosis factor (TNF), complement and heat shock proteins

questions.question: A patient presented with a fever and loose stool for one week. He was diagnosed with typhoid infection. Which of the following MHC class is responsible for antigen presentation in this patient?

explanation.text: In a patient with typhoid infection (caused by Salmonella typhi), antigen presentation primarily involves MHC class II molecules, which present antigens derived from extracellular pathogens to activate an immune response. Class I MHC class I molecules present endogenous antigens derived from intracellular pathogens, such as viruses and some bacteria.

Class II MHC class II molecules present exogenous antigens derived from extracellular pathogens, such as Salmonella typhi, the bacterium responsible for typhoid fever. Class III MHC class III molecules are not involved in antigen presentation. They encode components of the complement system and other immune-related molecules.

Non-MHC-dependent antigen presentation While non-MHC-dependent antigen presentation can occur through mechanisms like CD1 molecules presenting lipid antigens. Class II MHC molecules are expressed on the surface of antigen-presenting cells (APCs), such as dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells. These cells process exogenous antigens derived from extracellular microbes and proteins after internalization into endosomes or lysosomes.

The internalized proteins are broken down into peptides and associated with class II MHC in the vesicles and transported to the cell surface as stable peptide-MHC complexes. The class II-peptide complex is recognized by CD4+/helper T cells. Class II MHC molecules present antigens derived from extracellular pathogens to CD4+ helper T cells, initiating an immune response.

questions.question: Which component functions as the antigen binding site in MHC complexes 1 and 2, respectively?

options.A: MHC 1 - beta microglobulin; MCH 2 - alpha 3 domain
options.B: MHC 1 - alpha 1 and 2; MHC 2 - alpha 1 and beta 1
options.C: MHC 1 - alpha 1 and beta 1; MHC 2 - alpha 1 and 2
options.D: MHC 1 - invariant chain; MHC 2 - beta microglobulin

explanation.text: In MHC class I molecules, the alpha 1 and beta 1 domains together form the antigen-binding site, which binds to peptides derived from intracellular proteins. MHC-1 molecules are expressed on all nucleated cells, antigen-presenting cells, and platelets Mature RBCs that lack a nucleus don't express MHC-1 They are heterodimers with a polymorphic α or heavy chain linked non-covalently to a smaller β2-microglobulin.

The antigen is bound within a groove between the α1 and α2 domains of the alpha chain. This, along with the β2-microglobulin, forms a stable complex to be displayed on the cell surface. In MHC class II molecules, similar to MHC class I, the antigen-binding site is also formed by the alpha 1 and beta 1 domains, binding peptides derived from extracellular proteins presented by antigen-presenting cells.

They consist of 2 alpha and 2 beta chains of equal length. The invariant chain is a protein structure associated with MHC-2. It is associated with MHC-2 within endosomes to prevent the binding of endogenous antigens. The invariant chain is later broken down, while MHC-2 is moved to the cell surface.
